text:
The Ship of Men

By the time I was thirteen, I had learned to read my father's wardrobe the way other kids learned to read weather. The linen shirts meant brunch with the "boys"—an ever-shifting constellation of men named David, Marco, and one unforgettable person called Kip who owned a parrot that swore in Portuguese. The polo shirts, tucked in, meant a fundraiser. The leather jacket, which creaked like an old saddle and smelled faintly of vetiver cologne, meant a night out that would end with me falling asleep on someone's sofa while Donna Summer played in another room.

My father came out when I was eight, which is to say he sat me down on the edge of his bed one Saturday and told me he was going to start being honest about who he loved, and I said, "Does that mean I get a dog?" I did not get a dog. I got a stepfather-adjacent person named Luis, then no Luis, then a rotating cast of men who were unfailingly kind to me, who remembered my favorite ice cream and helped with my math homework in ways that suggested they, too, had once been defeated by fractions.

My mother had moved to Phoenix and collected turquoise and grievances. I stayed in the brownstone in Brooklyn with Dad, and I want to be clear that I was not neglected, or damaged, or any of the things the guidance counselor seemed to be hunting for with her careful questions. I was loved extravagantly. I was also, sometimes, lonely in a way that had no name yet—the loneliness of being the only girl in a world built entirely of men.

I should explain about my father's illness, because it sat underneath everything that year like a stone under a garden. He'd been sick on and off since before I could remember, kept upright by a daily chemistry of pills arranged in a plastic organizer with little doors labeled by day. By the spring of my thirteenth year, the medicine had begun to lose its argument with the disease. He tired easily. His hands, which had once spun me around the kitchen to Prince, trembled when he poured coffee. He never said the word dying. He said, "We're going on a trip," with the forced brightness of a man buying time by the week.

The trip was a cruise. Not an ordinary cruise—my father did nothing ordinarily—but a seven-day sailing out of Fort Lauderdale on a ship chartered, stem to stern, by and for gay men. Two thousand of them, more or less. And me.

"You can't be serious," I said, when he showed me the brochure. "I'll be the only kid. I'll be the only girl."

"You'll be the most popular person on the boat," he said. "Every one of those men was once a thirteen-year-old who felt like the only one."

"It won't be the same."

"It never is," he said. "But it's never nothing, either."

We boarded on a Sunday in April. The ship was called the Meridian Star, and it smelled of coconut sunscreen and new carpet. The check-in staff did a double take at my father and me, but my father produced some paperwork and a smile that had gotten him through many stranger doors, and up we went to a cabin with a balcony and a bathroom small enough to require choreography.

I spent the first day in a state of sullen vigilance, braced for humiliation. What happened instead was stranger and better: nothing. Nobody made it weird. A drag queen in the elevator—a vision in aquamarine, six foot four in her heels—looked down at me and said, "Honey, I love a sensible sandal," and kept reading her phone. At dinner, our tablemates were two couples, one from Chicago, one from Melbourne, who fought politely over who got to ask me about school, and then told me, in enormous detail, about their Labradoodle.

It took me about thirty-six hours to understand what the ship actually was. To the world outside, it was a party—there was a foam party, a disco night, a party whose theme I never fully decoded but that involved a great deal of glitter. But underneath, the ship was something else: a place where a few thousand men were being, for one week, unguarded. They held hands in the buffet line. They danced with their eyes closed. Old couples sat on the promenade deck at sunset doing absolutely nothing, together, in public, as though that were the whole point of the voyage. I had grown up around my father's friends, so I thought I knew what gay men were like. But I had only ever seen them in ones and twos, islands. On the Meridian Star I saw them as a sea, and I understood, dimly, the way you understand weather from inside it, that my father's whole life had been a negotiation between the island and the sea.

And me? I became, as my father predicted, inexplicably popular. I was simply the girl on the ship, and the ship had decided, collectively and without discussion, to adore me. Men taught me to play blackjack with cocktail napkins for chips. A retired hairdresser from Tampa braided my hair on the pool deck while four of his friends offered conflicting advice. On karaoke night, a bear of a man with a gray beard down to his sternum sang "I Will Always Love You" directly to me with such operatic sincerity that the entire lounge applauded and I had to pretend to have something in my eye.

My father watched all of this from deck chairs, wrapped in a blanket even in the heat, smiling the way you smile at a garden you planted but won't see bloom. He was conserving himself. He rationed his energy like a man paying for one thing at a time, and I noticed that the thing he was saving for kept not arriving, and I understood not to ask.

The boy appeared on Tuesday.

His name was Eli, and he was fourteen, and he was on the ship under circumstances nearly as improbable as mine: his uncle, a piano player in one of the lounges, had brought him along after Eli's parents' divorce had detonated his summer plans. We met at the soft-serve machine, which is where all meaningful meetings between teenagers occur, when the machine jammed and we both stood there shaking it in silent solidarity until it surrendered a ribbon of vanilla.

"You're the girl," he said.

"You're a boy," I said, which was the best I could do, because something had happened to my vocabulary.

He was sunburned across the nose and wore a T-shirt for a band I pretended to know. We sat by the pool and I waited for the familiar performance to begin—the boys at school were all elbows and volume and cruelty worn as a joke. It never came. Eli talked to me the way the men on the ship talked to each other: plainly, as if there were no audience. He told me he missed his dad and also couldn't stand him. He asked me what it was like, having a gay father, and instead of the polished answer I gave guidance counselors, I told him the truth: that it was ordinary and it was lonely, that I loved my father more than anyone on earth and sometimes wanted, with a ferocity that shamed me, for him to be someone simpler.

"That's not mean," Eli said. "That's just true."

No one had ever handed a thing back to me like that—taken my ugly confession, examined it, and returned it undamaged. We talked until the pool deck emptied and the sky went the color of a bruise healing. It was, and I say this with the full authority of my adult life, the first real conversation I ever had with a boy. Everything after—every date, every flirtation, my entire marriage, in some ways—has been measured against the soft-serve machine and a sunburned boy who listened.

We spent the next two days together in the easy way of shipboard friendships, which are entire relationships compressed into the length of a song. We played ping-pong. We judged the karaoke from the back row. We did not hold hands, though I thought about his hand approximately once every eleven seconds. On Thursday he walked me back to my cabin and said, "My uncle says this ship is the only place he ever felt normal," and then he said, "I get it," and then he said goodnight in a voice that cracked, which I treasured like a coin.

On Friday, my father got out of bed and put on the linen shirt.

"You're coming to the dance," he said. It was the last formal night. The ship's ballroom had been done up like a nineteen-forties nightclub, a band was playing standards, and the invitation had been circulating all week: the last dance of the cruise, for anyone who wanted one.

"Dad—"

"One dance," he said. "I have been on this earth long enough to know that you dance while you can."

He was so thin by then that the shirt hung off him like a sail in no wind. But he shaved, and he put on the vetiver, and when we walked into the ballroom I watched three hundred men turn and look at him and I saw what they saw: not a sick man but a brave one. His friends materialized from every corner—Marco, and the Davids, and the Tampa hairdresser, and Kip, mercifully parrotless—and they formed a kind of honor guard around us as the band played "The Way You Look Tonight."

My father held out his hand. I was thirteen and embarrassed and crying before we'd taken a single step.

We did not so much dance as sway, my hands on his shoulders, his at my waist, the way we had done a hundred times in the kitchen to Prince. He hummed along, badly, in my ear. He smelled of vetiver and underneath it, faintly, of medicine, and I understood with a clarity that arrived all at once, like a wave, that this was the last dance—not of the cruise, but of everything. He had spent the whole week saving himself for this. One dance was the price, and he had paid it gladly.

"I know," he said, into my hair, answering a question I hadn't asked.

"Don't," I said.

"One more thing," he said, and he held me a little tighter. "Look around, baby. Look at all of this. I needed you to see it. I needed you to know that wherever I am, I left you in a world full of people who will love you. You will never be the only one. Not on this ship, and not after."

The song ended. The ballroom erupted—two thousand men on their feet, and I understood that some portion of them knew, the way communities like that one always knew, had been watching each other leave for a generation and had perfected the art of saying goodbye without saying it. My father took a bow. He actually bowed, the ham, and the cheers doubled, and for a moment he stood there in the middle of it, thin and luminous and entirely himself, the island and the sea at once.

My father died four months later, at home, in the brownstone, on a morning in August. I won't linger there. The cruise was in April, and April is where I keep him.

But I will tell you what happened after the dance, because it took me years to understand it. Word had gone around the ship. On Saturday, our last full day, I could not walk ten feet without a man stopping me—to shake my father's hand, to press my shoulder, to tell me a story about him that I had never heard: that my father had once talked a stranger off a ledge of despair at a bar in Providence; that he had paid for someone's medication, quietly, for a year; that he had danced, at some legendary party in 1989, until the police came and then kept dancing. He had never told me any of it. He had given me the cruise instead—so that I could learn who he was from the people who loved him, in the one place where that love could be fully visible.

Eli found me at the soft-serve machine that night. We didn't talk much. He gave me an email address on a napkin that I lost in the Fort Lauderdale airport, which I grieved for a while and then decided was right—some things are supposed to stay exactly where and when they happened.

We docked on Sunday. The men dispersed into taxis and airports and lives, back to the islands, and I watched them go with the strange grief of leaving a country I had only just learned to name. My father was exhausted beyond speech and slept the entire flight home, and I held his trembling hand in both of mine, and the flight attendant brought an extra blanket and didn't charge us for the headphones, and the world was briefly and entirely kind.

I am older now than my father was on that ship. Every time a ship's band strikes up I am thirteen again, swaying in a ballroom full of men, my father's cologne in my hair, the whole sea of them around us, cheering. My mother still collects turquoise and grievances in Phoenix. Kip's parrot, I am told, is alive and still swearing in Portuguese. And every few years, at a wedding or a fundraiser or once, memorably, in a hardware store, a man about my father's age will look at me twice and say, "Wait—were you the girl on the Meridian Star?" And I say yes, and they tell me something new about my father, and it is like finding one more door in the pill organizer, one more day I didn't know he'd saved for me.

The last dance, he called it. He was wrong about that, in the end. It was the last one for him. It was the first one for me.
